# Shaping a performance {#sec-performance}

Once a part has the right notes, its character depends on timing, articulation
and dynamics. Modal offers two places to shape them: edits to the stored events
and settings applied while a track plays. Choosing between them keeps the
relationship between what is seen, heard and exported understandable.

## Stored edits and playback settings

A transform changes the selected music and is an undoable edit. For example,
transposing a phrase changes its stored pitches. The piano roll and event
list then show those new pitches.

A playback setting instead leaves the events intact. A track's transpose,
velocity offset, time offset and playback quantise can alter what is heard
without rewriting the performance. This suits comparison or compensation
for a particular instrument. The track settings make these changes visible;
the event list continues to show the original events.

MIDI export writes stored events, not the result of all playback settings.
To make a playback change part of the exported performance, freeze it first,
as described at the end of this chapter.

## Three routes to a transform

Transforms use the editing language's targets. There are three useful routes:

- `!` takes a range or object first, then offers a transform. For example,
  `!ib` chooses this bar before choosing how to change it.
- `, x` chooses the transform first, then its target. It is useful when the
  desired operation is already clear.
- A named `:` command takes the Visual selection, or otherwise the current
  bar. It can specify exact arguments and be found through the palette.

A transform that needs several parameters asks for them in turn. Enter takes
the displayed default; Tab offers choices where available. Parameters already
supplied at the command line need not be entered again. This makes a named
command such as `:quantize 1/8 swing=60` an entry into the same operation,
not a separate system to learn.

The reference in @sec-transform-reference lists command syntax and parameter
defaults. The following sections explain the musical distinctions behind them.

## Quantising timing

**Quantising** moves notes towards a rhythmic grid. The simple `q` operator
quantises starts to the track's editing grid. The extended quantise transform
also offers a grid, strength, swing and the choice of starts, ends, both or
lengths.

Strength controls how far a note moves towards its target. At 100% it reaches
the target; a smaller percentage retains some of the played deviation.
Swing changes the spacing of alternating subdivisions: 50% is straight,
while a later second subdivision creates a long-short pair. Modal accepts
25% to 75%, allowing the opposite feel too.

The choice of what moves matters. Quantising starts places attacks;
quantising ends controls release points; quantising lengths changes durations.
These decisions can produce different articulation even when the same grid
is used. A passage of detached notes should not acquire an unintended legato
merely because its starts were corrected.

Pedalling can follow the moved notes, retain its original timing or ask each
time, according to `quantizepedal`. The default is `follow`. The extended
quantise dialogue asks about the pedalling explicitly. Notes that cannot
move safely because of a collision can remain in place and be reported;
read the result rather than assuming every requested target was reached.

### Playback quantise

The track's Q setting applies quantise while it plays. Its grid can follow
the editing grid or remain fixed; strength, swing and the kind of movement
are track settings too. `, t q` toggles it. In the Tracks view, Enter on the
Quantise column opens these parameters in the inspector, edited as any
inspector is (@sec-inspector-editing). Each change is heard at once while
the song plays, so a strength or swing can be judged before it is kept.

`, T q` bypasses playback quantise across tracks for comparison. The piano
roll can mark the positions where notes will actually be heard, using
`quantizemarks` (`, T m`). Stored and heard positions remain distinct until
the transform is frozen.

## Velocity and musical dynamics

**Velocity** is the note-on value sent to the instrument, usually affecting
loudness, attack or timbre. The `^` operator accepts three kinds of change:
`80` sets a value, `+10` adds an amount and `80%` scales the existing values.
Their musical purposes differ: setting makes a uniform passage; adding
brightens it while keeping differences; scaling changes its dynamic range.

The velocity transforms provide more specific shapes:

| Transform | Musical purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Lift / lower | Move a percentage of the way towards the upper limit or the velocity floor |
| Limit | Keep values within a low-high range |
| Ramp | Create a rise or fall across the phrase, using absolute values or percentages |
| Compress / expand | Reduce or increase differences about a chosen centre over a moving window |
| Phrase | Change the size of the phrase's dynamic shape over time |
| Chord accent / balance | Bring out top notes or shape the balance from low to high |
| Chord compress / expand | Change the spread of velocities within each chord |

For example, a `60-100` velocity ramp specifies endpoints, while `80%-120%`
changes each note relative to its own velocity as the ramp progresses.
The second retains more of the original differences between simultaneous notes.

`velclip` controls relative changes near the limits. Its default, `soft`,
eases them towards the boundary rather than flattening every high note at
the ceiling; `hard` clips. `velfloor` sets the lower bound, initially 1.
A MIDI note-on velocity of zero is not used as an ordinary quiet note.

The velocity lane offers direct local editing alongside these phrase-level
operations; see @sec-controllers.

## Pitch and harmony

Chromatic transposition changes every pitch by a number of semitones. It
preserves intervals but can change how a phrase relates to its harmony.
Key-aware transposition instead moves by scale degrees in a chosen key.
A phrase can move within D dorian while retaining the scale's unequal steps.
Notes outside the scale retain their distance above the scale note below.

The key is explicit for the operation, rather than a global promise that
all later editing follows a key. Names include forms such as `Eb`, `F#m`
and `D dorian`. Modal offers a fitting key from the target notes; Tab and
the offered alternatives help choose another interpretation. The musical
judgement remains yours, particularly for short or chromatic passages.

**Inversion** reflects pitches about a pivot. Chromatic inversion measures
semitones; key-aware inversion measures scale degrees. **Retrograde** reflects
the order of notes in time, reversing the rhythmic pattern. These are useful
ways to derive related material while keeping the source available through
copying and undo.

## Time, length and humanisation

**Stretch** changes timing about the target's first event. A ratio of `2`
doubles the time distances, giving half speed; `1/2` halves them, giving double
speed; `150%` multiplies them by one and a half. This is a performance edit,
not a change of the song's tempo map.

**Length** can set a note fraction or scale durations by a percentage.
**Legato** extends each note or chord towards the next, leaving the last
without a following target. It is useful for connected phrasing, whereas a
percentage length change suits shortening a part while retaining its rhythm.

**Humanise**, also available as `~`, adds bounded random changes in start time
and velocity. `humanizetime` and `humanizevel` set the limits, initially
10 ms and 8 velocity units. Random variation is a tool for creating variation;
it does not infer musical emphasis or replace a played performance's intention.

## Separating and redirecting material

A **split** sends notes above or below a chosen pitch to another track. This
can separate a keyboard part into registers with different sounds. The
transform asks for the split note, side and destination; a new destination
name creates a track.

**Remap** changes a note pitch or controller number, for example redirecting
modulation data from `cc1` to expression on `cc11`. Controller numbers are
addresses; their effect depends on the receiver. Changing the address is
not the same as scaling its values.

**Filter** deletes events matching a search query. Its name means filtering
material out, not merely hiding it from view. The current search can supply
the query, allowing matches to be inspected before deletion.

**Thin** reduces the density of continuous controller, bend and aftertouch
data. Its density and value-step controls are useful for simplifying a dense
recorded gesture. It excludes pedals. In this edition it should not be
assumed to preserve every intermediate return to zero; inspect important
reset events after thinning.

## Playback offsets and instrument setup

A playback **transpose** or **velocity offset** changes what a track sends
without rewriting its notes. Notes transposed beyond MIDI's pitch range are
not sent and are reported. Velocity offsets stay within valid note-on values.

A **time offset** changes when all the track's events are sent. Negative
milliseconds can compensate for a slow attack; a musical fraction instead
expresses a rhythmic displacement. The Tracks field accepts milliseconds,
ticks and musical fractions, including composites such as `+1/16-22t`.
The chosen units retain their meaning through saving and loading.

Bank MSB, Bank LSB and Program supply an instrument setup at playback start.
An unset field is shown as `-`; clearing it removes that request. Program
and bank values use MIDI numbers from 0 to 127. Some instruments label their
patches from 1 to 128, so consult the instrument's numbering when choosing a
sound. Program changes stored among events can change the sound later in the song. A dot
after Program identifies such changes; conflicting setups on a shared port
and channel are warned about because the instrument receives one stream of
messages, not isolated virtual instruments for each Modal track.

## Freezing a playback decision

**Freeze**, `, t f` or `:track-freeze`, commits playback changes to stored
events and resets the chosen settings. It is useful when a comparison has
become a decision, or when another MIDI program must hear the same result.
The choices are All, Transpose, Velocity, Quantise and Time offset.

Playback must be stopped. Freeze takes the current whole track, or selected
whole rows in Tracks, as one undoable edit. Other Visual selections must
be left first. The choice list explains unavailable operations rather than
silently dropping part of the request.

All freezes quantise before the time offset. Time offset alone requires
quantise to be off; freeze quantise first or choose All. Quantise cannot be
committed while the relevant playback quantise is bypassed. A zero offset
or a retained but disabled quantise setting is not an active change to freeze.

The complete proposed edit is validated before it is applied. Out-of-range
pitches, invalid times and new collisions can refuse it. Millisecond offsets
use the current tempo map when converted into stored musical positions.
Undo restores both the events and the settings, keeping the two accounts of
the performance consistent.
